confound

kuhn-FOWND · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To confound is to cause confusion or bewilderment in someone.

The riddle at the escape room's final door confounded every team that attempted it that weekend.

Worked Example

The auditors were confounded by the company's books, which somehow balanced perfectly despite three years of missing receipts.

Confound describes a deep, often frustrating confusion -- something that genuinely stumps a person, not just a passing question.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

baffle: To baffle is to block every attempt at understanding -- a baffled person keeps trying angles, and every one fails. Confound adds heat and disorder to the same wall: it frustrates and scrambles, upending what you thought you knew. Both leave the problem unsolved and the person still working at it.

perplex: To perplex is to tangle someone in uncertainty -- a perplexed person keeps turning the problem over, unsure which way to go. To confound hits harder: it stumps and frustrates, leaving no promising direction at all. Perplexity is a knot you are still working; confounding defeats the effort.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

clarify: to make something clear and easier to understand

enlighten: to give someone greater understanding

Where it sits · how completely it scrambles your thinking — puzzle → confound → stupefy

puzzle vs. confound: Puzzle describes a milder curiosity or confusion, without the deep frustration that confound often implies.

stupefy vs. confound: Stupefy goes further than confound, describing a confusion so total it leaves someone stunned and unable to think at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — con-

Prefix — con-: with, together (intensifying) (Latin)

Root — found

Root — found: to pour, to mix together (from Latin fundere, 'to pour' -- not the found of finding or founding)

Put it together

Put it together: Confound comes from Latin confundere ('to pour together, to mix up'): con- ('together,' intensifying) + found (from fundere, 'to pour'). It's the exact same Latin ancestor as the everyday word confuse, just borrowed into English twice, through two different paths.

Use the root in a new word: confuse

Use the root in a new word: confuse: Two nearly identical road signs confuse drivers at the exit every single day.

Root Check

Word Choice

Confound and confuse share the exact same Latin ancestor, confundere -- English just borrowed the word twice, once through French (confound) and once directly from Latin (confuse). They're practically cousins.
